title: Descriptive analysis of TikTok content on vaccination in Arabic
screen_reason: QUALITY-ONLY study. The 129 Arabic-language vaccination TikTok videos were scored with a 3-item mini-DISCERN instrument (1 = poor to 5 = excellent) covering balance/bias, scientific description of benefits and risks, and presence of clear misinformation. Every result is reported as a MEAN score (by creator category, video topic, year, country dialect) or as a regression coefficient / Kendall's tau correlation. Although the authors defined a 'lower quality (1.00-3.00)' vs 'higher quality (3.01-5.00)' dichotomy, they never report the number or share of videos falling in either band, and never report a share of videos coded as containing misinformation. Per INSTRUCTIONS section 3, a Likert accuracy scale reported only as a mean is not a share and yields no row; and per section 1 a QUALITY-only study is excluded.
missed_or_uncertain: Numbers seen but NOT extracted, with reasons. (a) Mean mini-DISCERN scores: overall by creator category HCP 4.818 +/- 0.726 vs Media 4.053 +/- 1.441 vs Lay individuals 2.003 +/- 1.641 (P < 0.001); by topic COVID-19 vaccination 2.542 +/- 1.827 vs childhood vaccination 4.510 +/- 1.269 vs general vaccination 3.444 +/- 1.895 vs other vaccines 4.705 +/- 0.911 (P < 0.001); also by year and by country dialect (Table 2). These are scale MEANS on a quality instrument, not shares of videos, so no row (INSTRUCTIONS section 2 'scale MEANS only' exclusion, section 3 DISCERN rule). (b) Sample-composition percentages: creator category HCP 56 (43.4%), Lay 51 (39.5%), Media 22 (17.1%); topic COVID-19 59 (45.7%), childhood 35 (27.1%); country-of-dialect distribution (Egypt 43, KSA 16, etc.). These describe WHO posted and about WHAT, not what share of content was false, so they are not prevalence estimates. (c) Screening counts: 200 videos retrieved, 3 off-topic, 68 duplicates, 129 unique retained - a flow diagram, not a falsity share. JUDGEMENT CALL for an adjudicator: mini-DISCERN item 3 ('Does the video contain clear misinformation regarding vaccination?') is a veracity item, and the authors did operationalise misinformation ('demonstrably false or unsupported claims about vaccines, such as those related to safety, efficacy, or conspiracy theories'). If the review's convention were to retain a QUALITY row carrying a scale_score value, this paper would supply one row per creator category or topic with value_kind = scale_score. I did not create such rows because no share of videos is recoverable from the text and the paper would in any case be excluded from prevalence.

rob.design: Cross-sectional descriptive content analysis. Ten predefined Arabic vaccination keywords were typed into the TikTok search bar with video-only filtering, from two locations (Jordan and Kuwait); the top 5 videos per keyword were collected independently by four authors between 12 and 15 July 2024. 200 videos retrieved; 3 off-topic and 68 duplicates removed, leaving 129 unique videos posted 2 Jan 2021 - 10 Jul 2024. Quality rated independently by two subject-expert raters (a clinical virology consultant and a clinical pharmacy associate professor) on a 3-item mini-DISCERN (1-5), averaged. Inter-rater agreement Cohen kappa = 0.747 (SE 0.047), 0.900 (SE 0.035) and 0.923 (SE 0.032) for the three items, all P < 0.001. No response rate applies. Non-parametric tests (Kruskal-Wallis, Mann-Whitney), Kendall tau, and linear regression (R2 = 0.534).
rob.item6_quote: Each item on the mini-DISCERN was rated on a scale from 1 (poor quality) to 5 (excellent quality), and the exact items were: (1) Is the video balanced and unbiased? (2) Does the video scientifically describe the benefits/risks of vaccination? and (3) Does the video contain clear misinformation regarding vaccination? Here, we operationalized the term “misinformation” by identifying content that included demonstrably false or unsupported claims about vaccines, such as those related to safety, efficacy, or conspiracy theories [38,39].
rob.item10_quote: Of 200 videos, three videos were unrelated to the topic of vaccination in humans (one on veterinary vaccines and two were on future epidemics/outbreaks), and 68 videos were duplicates. Consequently, the final study sample of TikTok videos comprised 129 unique videos (Figure 2).
